title: Delete a Node at a Given Position in a Linked List
directAnswer: To delete index k, walk to its predecessor (index k − 1) and relink past the target: prev.next = prev.next.next. Position 0 is the special case — there's no predecessor, so return head.next as the new head. O(n) time, O(1) space.

remember.pattern: Walk to predecessor, relink past the target (prev.next = prev.next.next)
remember.formula:
if position == 0: return head.next
prev = head
repeat position - 1 times: prev = prev.next
prev.next = prev.next.next
return head
rules: To delete index `k`, stop on index `k − 1` — walk `position − 1` steps to reach the predecessor.
Relink with `prev.next = prev.next.next` — this skips the target so it's no longer reachable.
Position `0` has no predecessor: **return `head.next`** as the new head (don't try to walk).
The head can change (deleting index 0), so the function must **return the head**.
Read `prev.next` before relinking; deleting the head and an empty list are the two boundary cases to name.
whenToUse: Remove the node at a known 0-based index from a singly linked list
Drop an element while keeping the rest of the chain intact
Any 'unlink one node' subproblem (remove duplicates, remove by value)
Cleanup steps inside larger list rewrites
antiSignals: You only have a reference to the node to delete, not its predecessor, and it isn't the tail → copy the next node's value and skip it instead
You delete from the front repeatedly → that's an O(1) pop-head, no walk needed
Random index deletes happen constantly → an array or balanced structure may fit better
It's a doubly linked list with the node in hand → unlink in O(1) using prev/next directly
remember.takeaway: Deletion is the mirror of insertion: reach the predecessor, then rewire one link to bypass the target. Get the walk-to-position-minus-one and the head-delete case right and remove-by-value and remove-duplicates fall out of the same skeleton.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you reach the predecessor (index − 1), relink past the target without losing the rest of the list, and treat deleting the head as a separate case that changes the returned head.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Walking to the target node itself instead of its predecessor, or not handling position 0 and dereferencing a null predecessor.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Name the two invariants: stop one node early, and relink prev.next = prev.next.next. Call out that position 0 returns head.next, which is why the function returns a head.

problemStatement:
You are given the `head` of a singly linked list and an integer `position` (0-based).

Delete the node at index `position` and return *the head of the modified list*.

You may assume `0 ≤ position < length`, so a node always exists at that index.
constraints: The list is singly linked (next pointers only)
understanding: Removing index k means the node before it should point to the node after it, bypassing the target so it drops out of the chain. Index 0 has no predecessor, so deleting it just advances the head to the second node.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is position 0-based?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Deleting position 0 removes the head; position length − 1 removes the tail.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is position guaranteed to be a valid index?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, 0 ≤ position < length, so a node always exists there. I won't walk off the end, but I still special-case the head.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What should I return if deleting the only node?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: head.next, which is null — an empty list. The position-0 branch handles it.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I free the deleted node?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: In Java/Python the garbage collector reclaims it once nothing references it; unlinking is enough. In a manual-memory language I'd free it explicitly.

examples.explanation: Walk position − 1 = 0 steps → predecessor is node 1. Relink: 1.next = 1.next.next (node 3).
No predecessor: return head.next (node 2) as the new head.
Deleting the only node returns head.next = null — an empty list.

diagrams.title: Picking the right branch
diagrams.caption: Deleting the head is the only special case; everything else walks to position − 1 and relinks past the target.

approaches.name: Iterative — Walk to Predecessor, Then Relink (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: Lead with this. It's the canonical delete and mirrors insert-at-position.
hints: To unlink the node at index k, which node's next pointer do you actually have to change — the target's, or the one before it?
Reaching index k − 1 takes k − 1 steps. What do you do when k is 0 and there's no node before the target?
Once you're on the predecessor, how do you make the target disappear from the chain with a single pointer assignment?
approaches.complexityReasoning: At most position − 1 ≤ n − 1 steps to reach the predecessor, then O(1) relink. No extra structures → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
We reach the node just before the target and rewire its `next` to jump over the target.

**Why the predecessor.** In a singly linked list you remove a node by editing the `next` of the node before it. So to delete index `k`, get a handle on index `k − 1` and set its `next` to the target's `next`. That's why we walk `position − 1` steps, not `position` — landing on the target itself gives you no way to bypass it.

**The relink, in one line.** Standing on `prev`, do `prev.next = prev.next.next`. `prev.next` is the target; `prev.next.next` is the node after it. After the assignment, nothing points to the target, so it's unreachable and gets garbage-collected. The rest of the list is untouched.

**Why deleting the head is special.** Index 0 has no predecessor — there's no `prev.next` to edit. Instead the head advances: return `head.next`. This is exactly why the function returns a head; only the head-delete changes it, and the caller must learn the new head.

**Why the loop is counted.** We stop at a fixed index, so a `for` loop of `position − 1` iterations lands precisely on the predecessor. A condition-driven walk to the tail would overshoot.
approaches.insight: Deletion is insertion run backward: instead of saving the tail and splicing in, you read past the target and relink over it. The named trap is the head-delete case — forget it and you dereference a null predecessor or fail to advance the head.

dryRun.intro: position is 2, so walk position − 1 = 1 step to the predecessor (node 2), then relink past node 3.

java.explanation: No predecessor at index 0 — deleting the head just advances it.
Second node becomes the new head (null if the list had one node).
Walk position − 1 steps to stop on the predecessor, not the target.
Bypass the target so nothing references it — it's unlinked.
Head is unchanged for any position > 0.

python.explanation: Advance the head past the deleted first node.
Counted walk lands exactly on the predecessor.
Relink over the target node to remove it.

diagrams.title: Walk to predecessor, relink past the target
diagrams.caption: prev moves position − 1 steps; one assignment drops node 3 out of the chain.

pitfalls: Walking position steps instead of position − 1 — you land on the target and can't bypass it.
Not handling position 0 — dereferences a null predecessor or fails to advance the head.
Forgetting to return the head — a head delete never reaches the caller.
Assuming position may be out of range — here it's guaranteed valid, but in general validate it.

edgeCases.behavior: Head delete: return head.next = null → empty list.
Walk 1 step to node 2; prev.next.next is null; prev.next = null removes the tail → [1, 2].

approaches.name: Dummy Head — Uniform Delete Without the Special Case
approaches.whenToMention: Offer as a clean way to erase the position-0 branch; interviewers like the dummy-node idiom.
hints: What if a fake node sat in front of the real head so that even the head has a 'predecessor'?
Anchor prev on the dummy, walk position steps from there, then relink the same way.
Return dummy.next at the end — it tracks the real head whether or not you deleted index 0.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Same single walk of up to position ≤ n steps and an O(1) relink → O(n) time. One dummy node and a pointer → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
A dummy node placed before the head gives every real node a predecessor, including the original head — so the position-0 case stops being special.

**Why the dummy removes the branch.** With `dummy.next = head`, deleting index 0 is just relinking `dummy.next = dummy.next.next`, identical to deleting any other index. There's no longer a 'the head has no predecessor' exception, so one code path handles all positions.

**Walk count shifts by one.** Because `prev` starts on the dummy (one slot before the real head), we walk `position` steps (not `position − 1`) to reach the predecessor of index `position`. Then the relink `prev.next = prev.next.next` is the same.

**Return dummy.next.** The real head is always `dummy.next` after the operation — it equals the original head when we deleted elsewhere, or the second node when we deleted index 0. Returning it covers both without a branch.

**Trade-off.** Same O(n)/O(1) cost as the direct version, slightly more setup but no special case — a common pattern that pays off in problems with many edge cases (remove duplicates, remove by value).
approaches.insight: The dummy head turns 'the head is special' into 'the head is just another node'. It's the same sentinel trick used to build lists in Merge Two Sorted Lists, applied here to deletion.

dryRun.intro: dummy → 1 → 2 → 3. prev starts on dummy; walk position = 0 steps; relink past the head.

code.python:
def deleteNode(self, head: ListNode, position: int) -> ListNode:
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    prev = dummy
    for _ in range(position):
        prev = prev.next
    prev.next = prev.next.next
    return dummy.next

java.explanation: Sentinel before the head so the head gains a predecessor.
Start one slot earlier than before — that's why we walk position steps now.
position steps from the dummy lands on the target's predecessor.
Same relink for every index, including the original head.
The real head, correct whether or not we deleted index 0.

python.explanation: Fake node in front so no position is special.
prev begins on the dummy, one before the head.
Walk position steps to the predecessor.
dummy.next is the head in all cases.

diagrams.title: Dummy gives the head a predecessor
diagrams.caption: With D in front, deleting index 0 is the same relink as any other index.

pitfalls: Walking position − 1 steps from the dummy — off by one; from the dummy it's position steps.
Returning head instead of dummy.next — misses the new head when index 0 was deleted.
Forgetting to set dummy.next = head, leaving the dummy detached from the list.

commonMistakes: Walking to the target node instead of its predecessor.
Not handling position 0, then dereferencing a null predecessor.
Forgetting to return the head when the head was deleted.
Relinking with the wrong pointer (e.g. prev = prev.next.next) instead of prev.next = prev.next.next.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Stopping on the target instead of the predecessor
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Walking position steps lands you on the node to delete. From there you can't change the predecessor's next, so you can't unlink it cleanly. Stop at position − 1.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Ignoring the head-delete case
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Index 0 has no predecessor. Without the branch, walking position − 1 = −1 steps leaves prev on the head and deletes index 1, or a dummy-less relink dereferences null.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
prev = head
for _ in range(position - 1):
    prev = prev.next   # misbehaves when position == 0
prev.next = prev.next.next

patternNote: Walk-to-predecessor then relink-past-the-target — the deletion mirror of the insert splice. The dummy-head variant erases the head special case and is the same sentinel idiom used to build lists.
